Dataset composition therefore changes the effective objective: concentrating samples spatially increases M M , while changing subject count alters the balance of within- and cross-subject pairs in the kernel.

To isolate the role of cross-subject correspondences, one experiment ( E7 ) sets all cross-subject weights to zero. We refer to this modification as subject gating . We use encoders ViT-B, ViT-L, and ViT-H following the ViT-5 modernization of plain Vision Transformers ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Each input is tokenized into a 64 × 64 64\times 64 grid of 4096 4096 tokens, together with a class token and four register tokens ( Darcet et al., 2023 ) . All models train with AdamW ( Loshchilov & Hutter, 2018 ) at a constant learning rate 1 × 10 − 4 1\text{\times}{10}^{-4} on 64 to 256 NVIDIA GH200 accelerators (see sections B.3 and D.4 for details). The 93 runs consumed 316 000 316\,000 accelerator-hours over 7.32 7.32 million optimization steps and 94 200 94\,200 training exaFLOPs. Including the 124 linear probes, the study totals 349 000 349\,000 accelerator-hours. Across comparisons, the architecture family, optimizer, batch size, and evaluation protocol are held fixed, so experiments isolate changes in data composition, compute, or model capacity. Architecture dimensions, augmentations, optimizer settings, and FLOP accounting are given in Appendices B.1 and B.2 . 3.3 Experiments We organize the experiments around five factors, describing representation quality as S = f ⁡ ( P , C , N unique , B , ρ ) S=f(P,C,N_{\mathrm{unique}},B,\rho) . S S is macro-F1 on subjects excluded from both pretraining and probe training. P P denotes model capacity, C C compute measured in optimization steps, N unique N_{\mathrm{unique}} the number of distinct sample locations, B B the number of contributing sources, and ρ \rho the spatial coverage condition. Sources are individual subjects here, so B B is a subject count throughout the results. The data axes are not fully independent: at fixed N unique N_{\mathrm{unique}} , increasing B B necessarily reduces the mean number of locations per source N u ​ n ​ i ​ q ​ u ​ e / B N_{unique}/B .

Annotations indicate the fraction of M M contributed by cross-subject pairs before gating. At B = 2 B=2 , where cross-subject pairs contribute 49 % 49\% of M M , the gating contrast is unresolved. At B = 18 B=18 , where cross-subject pairs contribute 94 % 94\% of M M , gating reduces macro-F1 by 0.057 0.057 . Restricting a fixed sample budget to narrower anatomical coverage reduced representation quality at high subject count ( fig. 5 ). All B = 13 B=13 coverage conditions use the same thirteen coronal subjects, so the within-subset MDE of approximately 0.028 0.028 macro-F1 applies. Relative to every-10th-section sampling at B = 13 B=13 , macro-F1 decreased by 0.038 0.038 for four blocks, by 0.034 0.034 , 0.028 0.028 , and 0.021 0.021 for the three localized single-block conditions, and by 0.017 0.017 for 16 blocks. The four-block condition and two of the three localized conditions meet or exceed the MDE, while the 16-block condition and the remaining localized condition do not. Spatial concentration alone does not explain this ordering: the four-block condition spans 78 % 78\% of the full section range, yet shows the largest deficit, so the arrangement of covered and uncovered regions also contributes.

The primary contrast between 16 blocks and every-10th-section sampling matches both N unique N_{\mathrm{unique}} and positive weight M M and is unresolved, so introducing many small gaps into otherwise broad coverage has no detectable cost under this design. The deficit also appears only at high subject count, since no coverage condition differs detectably from every-10th-section sampling at B = 1 B=1 or B = 4 B=4 . Most coverage conditions also change the positive weight M M and thus do not isolate anatomical coverage as a single factor. At B = 13 B=13 , M M is 16.15 16.15 for every-10th-section sampling and 17.94 17.94 for 16 blocks, and ranges from 53.11 53.11 to 105.58 105.58 across the three localized conditions. The localized conditions therefore combine reduced coverage with a substantial change in objective composition, so this experiment does not separate the two contributions. Subject gating introduces an even larger change in positive weight. Cross-subject pairs supply 94.2 % 94.2\% of the positive weight at B = 18 B=18 , so removing them reduces M M by roughly a factor of 17, and performance under gating was lower from B = 4 B=4 onward. At B = 18 B=18 , macro-F1 decreased from 0.300 0.300 with the standard objective to 0.243 0.243 with gating, a difference of 0.057 0.057 that exceeds the within-subset MDE. Across the full-grid model, doubling positive weight is associated with an increase of β M = 0.0979 ​ [ 0.0597 , 0.1357 ] \beta_{M}=0.0979\,[0.0597,0.1357] in logit macro-F1, consistent with much of that deficit. Cross-subject anatomical correspondences therefore supply most of the positive mass available to SpatialNCE at high subject count and are important for maintaining performance in this regime. The composition of M M across E1 , E4 , and E7 , and the gating indicator after adjustment for M M , are detailed in sections D.2 and D.1 .

5 Discussion A central implication of our results is that the magnitude of source-level variation and the value of acquiring additional sources are distinct quantities. Inter-source variation strongly affects generalization, yet broader source sampling does not improve representations when it redistributes a fixed sample budget. For hierarchical datasets, observing substantial variation between sources therefore provides insufficient evidence for how additional acquisition effort should be allocated. The relevant quantity is the marginal value of samples from new versus already represented sources. This distinction extends the usual notion of data scale. A sample count alone does not specify whether dataset growth adds observations, sources, or coverage of the underlying domain, and our experiments show that these forms of scale can have different value within the same learning problem. Making this decomposition explicit provides a way to reason about data acquisition in settings with repeated or spatially structured observations, where collecting another sample and collecting another source can have very different costs. Our results establish this distinction in spatially supervised whole-brain histology and motivate treating data composition as an explicit dimension of empirical scaling studies. A.3 Downstream task and evaluation semantics The probe predicts one of 191 cytoarchitectonic areas from a class vocabulary fixed before evaluation and derived from the Julich Brain atlas ( Amunts et al., 2020 ) . Probe-training samples are capped at 1000 1000 per class without replacement; capped classes are filled round-robin across subjects, with a fixed-seed random order within each subject. The probe is a single affine layer mapping the frozen encoder representation to the 191 classes and is trained with categorical cross-entropy. Encoder features are passed to the classifier without normalization or other transformation. The probe is optimized with AdamW at a constant learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} and weight decay 0.05 0.05 , using a global batch size of 2048 2048 across 64 GH200 accelerators for 4710 4710 steps. The fixed step budget keeps probe optimization effort independent of training-pool size. No physical section contributes to both probe training and evaluation. Macro-F1 is computed separately for each evaluation subject over the classes present in that subject—137, 171, and 172 of the 191 classes for the three primary unseen subjects, respectively—and then averaged across subjects. Three subjects are excluded from all controlled pretraining runs and from probe training and form the primary unseen evaluation set. Three additional subjects are excluded from probe training but remain eligible for pretraining and define the transfer subjects.

The remaining annotated subjects contribute to probe training, with separate sections held out for evaluation. Generalization level is therefore defined for each model–subject pair. B.3 Software and execution environment All runs were executed on the JUPITER supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre. Its accelerated partition uses NVIDIA GH200 Grace–Hopper superchips with four accelerators per node. Pretraining used 16 nodes for ViT-B, 32 nodes for ViT-L, and 64 nodes for ViT-H, corresponding to 64, 128, and 256 accelerators, respectively. The global pretraining batch size was fixed at 2048 2048 across all capacities. Linear probes used 16 nodes with 64 accelerators. All pretraining and probe jobs ran under SLURM in the same Apptainer image, providing a common software environment across runs. Training used PyTorch ( Paszke et al., 2019 ) and distributed data parallel (DDP) training. Statistical analysis and figure generation were performed in a separate environment using NumPy, pandas, SciPy, and statsmodels. B.1 Architecture and optimization Encoders use the modernized ViT-5 architecture of Wang et al. (2026) , with SwiGLU feed-forward blocks of hidden size 8 / 3 8/3 times the embedding dimension, bias-free QKV projections, no stochastic depth, and four register tokens ( Darcet et al., 2023 ) . Each 2048 × 2048 2048\times 2048 input is divided into a 64 × 64 64\times 64 grid of 32 × 32 32\times 32 -pixel patches, yielding 4096 4096 patch tokens and a sequence length of 4101 4101 after adding the class token and four register tokens; the class token provides the encoder representation. A uniform predictor over the 191-class vocabulary yields 0.004 0.004 macro-F1 averaged across the three unseen subjects. Appendix E Remaining limitations The study has several limitations. The subject pool is finite, and subject subsets at different values of B B overlap, so comparisons across subject-count conditions are not based on fully independent sets of subjects. The primary evaluation uses three unseen subjects, although the main comparisons retain their direction under two additional held-out-subject assignments ( section D.5 ). Each configuration was pretrained with a single optimization seed because of the computational cost of the study. Replication across independently composed subject subsets captures sensitivity to subject selection but does not separately quantify optimization-seed variability. The coverage manipulation in E4 changes both sampled anatomy and the spatial distribution of pairwise relationships entering SpatialNCE. Subject gating in E7 directly changes the composition and total positive weight of the SpatialNCE objective. The corresponding results therefore do not isolate all contributing mechanisms individually, as discussed in section 4.4 . E1 evaluates fixed-sample subject scaling at a single budget of approximately 450 000 450\,000 unique locations and over B = 1 B=1 – 18 18 . Subject diversity may have a different effect at substantially smaller sample budgets or when each subject is sampled more sparsely. All downstream results use linear probes on frozen representations and cytoarchitectonic area labels. More expressive readouts may recover representation structure that is not linearly accessible, although the familiarity effect in section 4.1 shows that the linear probe is sensitive to substantial inter-subject differences.
